rm -f "$D/dest" "$D/argv"
cat > "$D/fakesudo" <<STUB
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "\$@" >> "$D/argv"
out=()
while [ \$# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "\$1" in
    -o|-g) shift 2 ;;
    *) out+=("\$1"); shift ;;
  esac
done
exec "\${out[@]}"
STUB
chmod +x "$D/fakesudo"
SUDO="$D/fakesudo" install_secret atticPullToken "$D/dest" 'machine attic.ko.ag password '
if [ -s "$D/argv" ] && ! grep -q SUPERSECRETVALUE "$D/argv"; then

else

    "argv=[$(cat "$D/argv" 2>/dev/null)] (empty means the install never ran, so this proved nothing)"
fi

input.new_string:
# An explicit GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS still wins, for the case where you
# are deliberately deploying with some other credential.
#
# ALLOW_EXECUTABLES is set alongside it rather than left to the caller. home.nix
# pairs those two for WIF, and the most natural way to use this override on a WIF
# host -- pointing it at a wif-hosts.json by hand -- would otherwise have Google's
# auth library refuse the executable-sourced credential. Setting it is harmless
# for a service-account key, which ignores it, so the pair stays together.
if [ -n "${GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS-}" ]; then
  echo "system/deploy: using GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS from the environment"
  export GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS
  export GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES="${GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES-1}"
else
  # mapfile rather than word-splitting: a credential path could contain spaces,
  # and these lines are KEY=VALUE pairs meant for `env`, not for the shell.
  #
  # No `||` on the mapfile, deliberately. mapfile's exit status is mapfile's own
  # and never the process substitution's -- the same trap the pacman_wants call
  # above documents -- so a `|| exit` there would be dead code claiming a check
  # it does not perform. A failed `nix eval` writes to stderr and nothing to
  # stdout, so it arrives here as an empty array, which the length test catches.
  mapfile -t sops_env < <(sops_env_for .. "$host")
  # Load-bearing beyond the error message: `export "${empty_array[@]}"` expands
  # to zero words, and bare `export` prints the whole environment and succeeds.
  [ "${#sops_env[@]}" -gt 0 ] || {
    echo "system/deploy: no sops.environment for $host — nix eval failed, or the host has none." >&2
    echo "system/deploy: nix's own error, if any, is above." >&2
    exit 1
  }
  export "${sops_env[@]}"
fi

content.text:
The correctness reviewer earned its keep. Findings and what I did:

**Important — fixed.** `$host` was assigned *inside* the `else` arm of the `SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES` guard (line 75), while my new sops block read it unconditionally. Under `set -u`, `SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES=1 ./system/deploy` — the documented way to re-run the non-package half — would abort on `host: unbound variable` after the `etc/` copy and before every credential it exists to install. My commit introduced that; the old line only used `$HOME`. Hoisted the assignment above the guard, with its `uname -n` rationale moved along.

**Test gaps — fixed, and mutation-checked.**
- No case asserted mode `600`. Deleting `-m600` passed all 9 tests while landing a world-readable attic token and SSH private key. Added a `stat` assertion; verified it fails when I remove `-m600`.
- Case "failed decrypt leaves file untouched" passed for the wrong reason — the stub staged both a non-zero exit *and* empty stdout, so the `[ -z "$val" ]` guard carried it. Now the stub emits `PARTIAL`; verified the case fails when I delete the exit-status check.
- Added a case for `sops_env_for` against a failing `nix`.

**Also fixed:** the dead `|| exit 1` on `mapfile` (its status is never the process substitution's — the repo already documents this exact trap 150 lines above, for `pacman_wants`), with the error message now saying the eval may have failed rather than blaming an empty `sops.environment`; and the explicit-`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` override now also sets `ALLOW_EXECUTABLES`, since splitting that pair would break the most natural way to use the override on a WIF host.

**Not fixed, flagged:** `mise.toml:49` still hardcodes the service-account key path, so `mise run sops` remains broken on `shiori` for the same root cause. Adjacent, not this commit's scope — want it in a follow-up?

My earlier suspicion about `mapfile` was right, but the reviewer established something I hadn't: the length guard isn't just a nicer error, it's load-bearing, because `export "${empty[@]}"` becomes bare `export`, which dumps the environment and *succeeds*.

input.content:
system/deploy: take the sops credential from the flake, and decrypt before installing

shiori has been building everything locally since the WIF migration. Every nix
invocation on it warns

  unable to download 'https://attic.ko.ag/kube/nix-cache-info': HTTP error 401

and then builds, because nix fails open on a substituter it cannot authenticate
to. That silently defeats the entire reason `hms` waits for CI: the switch is
supposed to be a download of the closure the runner already pushed to attic.

Two bugs, and the second is what kept the first quiet.

**The credential.** ./deploy hardcoded $HOME/.config/sops/gcp-key.json. shiori is
the sole WIF host, and the point of that migration is that it has no decryption
key on disk at all -- home.nix's wifHosts comment says so in as many words. So
sops could never decrypt there. home.nix already makes this choice per host, in
`sops.environment`, so ./secrets.sh now reads that back out of the flake instead
of keeping a second copy of the host list in bash. An explicit
GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS still wins, and carries ALLOW_EXECUTABLES with it
rather than splitting a pair home.nix deliberately keeps together.

One trap in doing that: the same attrset carries PATH="", which sops-nix sets for
sops-install-secrets' own sandboxed activation. Exporting it verbatim would blank
./deploy's PATH and break every command after the export, so it is dropped, and a
case pins that.

**The install pattern.** `sops ... | sed ... | sudo install /dev/stdin DEST` runs
its three stages concurrently, so install created and truncated DEST before sops
had finished failing, then exited 0 having written nothing. A failed deploy did
not leave the previous credential alone -- it replaced it with a 0-byte file that
looks provisioned. `set -euo pipefail` then stopped the script on that line, so
everything after it never ran. That is precisely the state shiori was in: a
0-byte /etc/determinate/netrc.custom, no /etc/nix/netrc at all (deploy writes it
two lines later), no mari builder key, and an unrestarted nix-daemon.

install_secret decrypts into a variable first and installs only on success, and
treats an empty decrypt as a failure rather than as something worth writing. The
plaintext still never reaches argv: it goes to install on stdin via bash's
builtin printf, since /proc/<pid>/cmdline is world-readable.

Also refuses a multi-line value where a line prefix was given -- a netrc entry is
one line, and prefixing only the first would leave a bare token on the second,
which curl parses happily and wrongly.

have broken: it was assigned inside the else arm of the SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES guard,

every credential it installs.

never the process substitution's, the same trap the pacman_wants call above
already documents. A failed `nix eval` arrives as an empty array instead, which
the length test catches -- and that test is load-bearing beyond its message,
because `export "${empty[@]}"` expands to zero words and bare `export` prints the
environment and succeeds.

mutation rather than assumption: removing -m600 fails the mode case, and removing

PATH, and a real decrypt through that env exits 0.

shiori from the wired-hosts list and still told you the deploy needs your
gcp-key.json.

path, so it remains broken on shiori for this same reason.

input.prompt:
Do a SECURITY code review of commit aec8243 in the git worktree /home/sauyon/devel/dotfiles/.claude/worktrees/deploy-wif-credentials. Review as a skeptic, not as the author. READ-ONLY: do not edit, write, or create any file in the repo, and do not run anything that changes state.

Range is `d3aa4555..HEAD` (one commit). Start with `git -C /home/sauyon/devel/dotfiles/.claude/worktrees/deploy-wif-credentials show aec8243`, then read the whole of `system/deploy`, `system/secrets.sh` and `tests/system-secrets.sh` — the new code depends on things defined far above it.

## Context

This repo is a PUBLIC Home Manager flake. `system/deploy` runs as the user, decrypts secrets from `secrets.yaml` with sops (GCP KMS), and `sudo install`s them into `/etc` root-owned 0600. The secrets in play are an attic binary-cache pull token and an SSH private key used by the nix daemon to reach a remote builder.

The commit replaces `sops … | sed … | sudo install /dev/stdin DEST` (which truncated DEST before knowing the decrypt succeeded) with a `install_secret` helper that decrypts into a shell variable first, and replaces a hardcoded GCP service-account key path with a per-host lookup of `homeConfigurations.<host>.config.sops.environment` from the flake.

## What I want scrutinised, from a security standpoint

Do not limit yourself to this list, and do not assume any item is actually a problem.

1. **Secret exposure surfaces.** The plaintext now lives in a bash variable and is written via builtin `printf` into `sudo install`'s stdin. Check every way it could leak: argv (`/proc/<pid>/cmdline`), environment (`/proc/<pid>/environ`), the filesystem (temp files, `/dev/stdin` semantics), shell tracing (`set -x`), core dumps, bash history, or the process table during the `sudo` call. Compare against the old pipeline — is the new shape strictly better, or does it trade one exposure for another?
2. **File modes and ownership, and the window between them.** `install -m600 -o root -g root /dev/stdin DEST` — is there an instant where DEST exists with a permissive mode and the secret already in it? Does `install` create-then-chmod or create-with-mode? Does it matter that DEST may already exist with different ownership?
3. **The `sudo install` invocation itself.** Anything an attacker who controls the environment (but not root) could do here — `SUDO`, `SOPS`, `NIX`, `JQ`, `SECRETS` are all overridable seams inherited from the ambient environment when deploy runs for real. Is that a meaningful escalation path, or is it equivalent to the pre-existing `PATH` exposure any script has? Note `pacman.sh` already established this seam convention.
4. **The flake-eval path.** `sops_env_for` runs `nix eval --json` on a repo-relative flake and feeds the result to `jq`, then the KEY=VALUE lines go to `export`. Could a malicious or malformed `sops.environment` inject something — a key name containing `=`, shell metacharacters, a newline in a value — such that `export "${sops_env[@]}"` does something unintended?   Read in full: `system/deploy`, `system/secrets.sh`, `tests/system-secrets.sh`, plus `system/pacman.sh`, `home.nix` (lines 30–90, 1686–1706), `mise.toml`, `docs/nix-binary-cache.md`.
  
  Two **Important** findings, five **nits**. No **Critical**. The core claim of the commit — decrypt-then-install, no plaintext in argv — holds up; the two Important findings are about what the commit *added around* it.
  
  ---
  
  ### 1. Important — `GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES` is defaulted on in the branch where the credential path is untrusted input
  
  `/home/sauyon/devel/dotfiles/.claude/worktrees/deploy-wif-credentials/system/deploy:261-265`
  
  ```bash
  if [ -n "${GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS-}" ]; then
    export GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS
    export GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES="${GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES-1}"
  ```
  
  That flag is not a compatibility toggle; it is the interlock Google shipped specifically because an `external_account` credential config contains `credential_source.executable.command`, an arbitrary command line that the auth library will `exec`. Default-off means "a credential config is data". Setting it to 1 means "a credential config is code".
  
  The two branches are not symmetric, and the commit treats them as if they were:
  
  - **Flake branch**: the value comes from `home.nix:1699-1702`, where `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` is `${wifCredentialConfig}` — a `pkgs.writeText` store path, immutable and root-owned. `home.nix`'s own comment is precise about why this is safe: *"The config above is a read-only store path, so this is a constraint, not a risk."*
  - **Override branch**: the path is whatever the operator typed on the command line. `home.nix`'s justification does not transfer, and this is exactly the branch that now turns the flag on by default.
  
  The in-tree comment does not say this. It says *"Setting it is harmless for a service-account key, which ignores it, so the pair stays together."* That is true and beside the point — the risk is not the service-account case, it is the `external_account` case, which is the only case where the flag does anything at all. Asked directly whether the tradeoff is documented honestly: no. The comment documents the benign half and omits that it is disabling a code-execution guard.
  
  Compounding it, `home.nix:71` records the prevailing mental model: *"Non-secret by construction (GCP documents credential configs as safe to commit)."* Credential configs really are treated as shareable, pasteable, commit-safe artifacts. With this flag on, a shareable artifact is a shell command.
  
  **Attacker model.** Someone who can get a JSON file in front of the operator, or into a location the operator will name — a config pasted into a chat/issue/agent transcript, a file downloaded during a bootstrap, a path under a directory the attacker can write (`/tmp`, a shared `~/Downloads`, a checkout of a third-party repo). They cannot run code as the operator. The operator runs the documented-looking `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/path/to/that.json ./system/deploy`.
  
  **Before this commit:** `sops` calls the auth library, the library refuses the executable-sourced credential (flag unset), deploy fails. **After:** the library runs `credential_source.executable.command` as the operator. So the override branch is genuinely opt-in per invocation, not the default path. That is what keeps this Important rather than Critical.

  `/home/sauyon/devel/dotfiles/.claude/worktrees/deploy-wif-credentials/system/secrets.sh:56,76`
  
  Going through the list you asked about, the new code is equal-or-better on every channel *except* shell tracing:
  
  | channel | old `sops \| sed \| sudo install` | new `install_secret` |
  |---|---|---|
  | argv (`/proc/<pid>/cmdline`) | clean | clean — `printf` is a builtin, `wc -l` gets it on a pipe. Verified by the test at `tests/system-secrets.sh:212-236`. |
  | environ (`/proc/<pid>/environ`) | clean | clean — `local val`, never exported |
  | filesystem / temp files | clean | clean — `$( )` uses a pipe, not a temp file (a here-string `<<<` *would* have used one; it isn't used) |
  | `/dev/stdin` semantics | pipe fd, root reads it | unchanged |
  | core dumps | in `sops`/`sed` address space | in `bash`'s address space — equivalent, both user-owned |
  | bash history | n/a | n/a |
  | process table during `sudo` | clean | clean |
  | **`set -x` / `SHELLOPTS=xtrace` / `BASH_XTRACEFD`** | **clean** | **full plaintext to stderr** |
  
  Confirmed empirically:
  
  ```
  $ bash -c 'set -x; v=$(echo SUPERSECRET); printf "%s%s\n" "pfx " "$v" | cat >/dev/null'
  ++ echo SUPERSECRET
  + v=SUPERSECRET
  + printf '%s%s\n' 'pfx ' SUPERSECRET
  ```
  
  So `bash -x system/deploy` — or `SHELLOPTS=xtrace ./system/deploy`, since bash imports `SHELLOPTS` from the environment — prints the attic pull token *and the mari SSH private key in full* to stderr. The old pipeline printed only `+ sops -d --extract ...` / `+ sed ...` / `+ sudo install ...`; the plaintext existed only inside pipes and never in the trace.
  
  **Attacker model.** Not a remote attacker: anyone who later reads the output. Concretely — deploy is a thing people debug with `bash -x` when it fails, and this repo's culture is to paste deploy output into commit messages, issues, and agent transcripts (this very commit message quotes deploy/nix output at length), and the repo is public. Also terminal scrollback on a shared/recorded session, a `tee`'d bootstrap log, and `BASH_XTRACEFD` pointed at a file. Result: full disclosure of a binary-cache pull token and a root-used SSH private key.

  `system/secrets.sh:76-77`

Separately, `nix-daemon` can read a half-written `/etc/nix/netrc` concurrently with the install.
  
  **Attacker model:** none; this is a reliability/fail-safety nit, not an attack. It matters only because the stated goal of the commit is "never leave a previously-good file worse". Writing to `DEST.tmp` and `mv`-ing would close it. Narrow enough that I would not block on it.
  
  ---
  
  ### 4. nit — the test's mode and ownership guarantees are weaker than the header claims
  
  `tests/system-secrets.sh:33-48, 142-151`
  
  Answering your question directly: the 0600 case **is** a true check for the property it asserts, but only for a subset of the real invocation.
  
  - **Ownership is untested, by construction.** The stub strips `-o`/`-g` and discards them. Changing `-o root -g root` to `-o nobody`, or deleting the flags entirely, passes all nine cases. Cheap fix: have the stub *record* `-o`/`-g` into `$D/argv` instead of silently dropping them, and assert they are `root`.
  - **Only the create path is mode-asserted.** The mode case runs right after `rm -f "$D/dest"`. The real-host path is overwrite-an-existing-file, and no case asserts the mode after an overwrite. (GNU `install` does chmod to the `-m` mode after copying, so the property holds — but the test does not establish it, and that is exactly what a test is for.) A case that pre-creates `$D/dest` at 0644 and asserts 600 afterwards would close it.
  - The argv case is sound and non-vacuous — `[ -s "$D/argv" ]` guards against the install never running, and staging output *plus* a nonzero exit in the `mksops 1 'PARTIAL'` case genuinely pins the exit-status check rather than letting the `-z` guard carry it. Good discipline.
  
  On your point 2 (the mode window) generally: no finding. GNU `install` sets `x->set_mode = true; x->mode = S_IRUSR|S_IWUSR` in `cp_option_init`, so a *newly created* destination is 0600 from the first byte and the final mode is chmod'd on after. For a *pre-existing* destination `install` writes into the existing inode and only chmods afterwards — so a pre-existing world-readable `/etc/nix/netrc` would hold the token at 0644 for the duration of the write. Creating such a file requires root, so this is below the reporting bar.
  
  ---
  
  ### 5. nit — `select(.key != "PATH")` is a one-entry denylist feeding `export`
  
  `system/secrets.sh:30-31`, `system/deploy:274-282`
  
  **I traced the quoting for injection and found none.** `mapfile -t` makes each jq output line exactly one array element; `"${sops_env[@]}"` expands to one word per element with no re-splitting, no glob, and no command substitution; and `export` is a builtin that assigns rather than evaluating. Specifically:
  - a key containing `=` (`{"A=B":"C"}`) → `export "A=B=C"` → sets `A` to `B=C`. No execution.
  - a key that is not a valid identifier (`{"a b":"1"}`) → `export` fails with *"not a valid identifier"*, returns 1, `set -e` aborts deploy. Fail-closed.
  - shell metacharacters or `$(...)` in a *value* → assigned literally, never expanded.
  - the one real caveat: a **newline** in a value splits into an extra array element, so `{"K":"a\nLD_PRELOAD=/evil.so"}` becomes two words and the second is exported as its own assignment. Still a plain `export`, not code execution.
  
  Which leads to the actual (mild) observation: PATH is filtered, but nothing else is. `LD_PRELOAD`, `BASH_ENV`, `IFS`, `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` and friends would all be exported into a shell that goes on to run `nix build`, `sudo`, `systemctl restart`. **This is not an escalation path** — the source is `home.nix` and the pinned flake inputs, and anyone who can change those can change `system/deploy` itself. But the justification given for filtering PATH is that `sops.environment` is written for a *different consumer* (`sops-install-secrets`, sandboxed, PATH="") and therefore may contain entries that are wrong here. That argument applies to the whole attrset, not just PATH. An allowlist (`GOOGLE_*`, `SOPS_*`, `AWS_*`, `VAULT_*`) is the same amount of jq and does not need revisiting when sops-nix adds a key.

  `system/secrets.sh:71`

  `system/secrets.sh:54` — `secrets=${SECRETS-../secrets.yaml}`

If the write fails partway — ENOSPC on `/`, the operator interrupting, `install` killed — DEST is left truncated or half-written, which is still "a working credential replaced by a broken one". Separately, `nix-daemon` can read a half-written `/etc/nix/netrc` concurrently with the install.
  
  **Attacker model:** none; this is a reliability/fail-safety nit, not an attack. It matters only because the stated goal of the commit is "never leave a previously-good file worse". Writing to `DEST.tmp` and `mv`-ing would close it. Narrow enough that I would not block on it.
  
  ---
  
  ### 4. nit — the test's mode and ownership guarantees are weaker than the header claims
  
  `tests/system-secrets.sh:33-48, 142-151`
  
  Answering your question directly: the 0600 case **is** a true check for the property it asserts, but only for a subset of the real invocation.
  
  - **Ownership is untested, by construction.** The stub strips `-o`/`-g` and discards them. Changing `-o root -g root` to `-o nobody`, or deleting the flags entirely, passes all nine cases. The comment concedes this (*"that the file lands root:root 0600 is ./deploy's business"*) while the case's own comment claims the check protects against *"publish[ing] the attic pull token and the mari SSH private key to every user on the box"* — ownership is half of that property and is not covered. Cheap fix: have the stub *record* `-o`/`-g` into `$D/argv` instead of silently dropping them, and assert they are `root`.
  - **Only the create path is mode-asserted.** The mode case runs right after `rm -f "$D/dest"`. The real-host path is overwrite-an-existing-file, and no case asserts the mode after an overwrite. (GNU `install` does chmod to the `-m` mode after copying, so the property holds — but the test does not establish it, and that is exactly what a test is for.) A case that pre-creates `$D/dest` at 0644 and asserts 600 afterwards would close it.
  - The argv case is sound and non-vacuous — `[ -s "$D/argv" ]` guards against the install never running, and staging output *plus* a nonzero exit in the `mksops 1 'PARTIAL'` case genuinely pins the exit-status check rather than letting the `-z` guard carry it. Good discipline.
  
  On your point 2 (the mode window) generally: no finding. GNU `install` sets `x->set_mode = true; x->mode = S_IRUSR|S_IWUSR` in `cp_option_init`, so a *newly created* destination is 0600 from the first byte and the final mode is chmod'd on after. For a *pre-existing* destination `install` writes into the existing inode and only chmods afterwards — so a pre-existing world-readable `/etc/nix/netrc` would hold the token at 0644 for the duration of the write. Creating such a file requires root, so this is below the reporting bar.
  
  ---
  
  ### 5. nit — `select(.key != "PATH")` is a one-entry denylist feeding `export`
  
  `system/secrets.sh:30-31`, `system/deploy:274-282`
  
  **I traced the quoting for injection and found none.** `mapfile -t` makes each jq output line exactly one array element; `"${sops_env[@]}"` expands to one word per element with no re-splitting, no glob, and no command substitution; and `export` is a builtin that assigns rather than evaluating. Specifically:
  - a key containing `=` (`{"A=B":"C"}`) → `export "A=B=C"` → sets `A` to `B=C`. No execution.
  - a key that is not a valid identifier (`{"a b":"1"}`) → `export` fails with *"not a valid identifier"*, returns 1, `set -e` aborts deploy. Fail-closed.
  - shell metacharacters or `$(...)` in a *value* → assigned literally, never expanded.
  - the one real caveat: a **newline** in a value splits into an extra array element, so `{"K":"a\nLD_PRELOAD=/evil.so"}` becomes two words and the second is exported as its own assignment. Still a plain `export`, not code execution.
  
  Which leads to the actual (mild) observation: PATH is filtered, but nothing else is. `LD_PRELOAD`, `BASH_ENV`, `IFS`, `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` and friends would all be exported into a shell that goes on to run `nix build`, `sudo`, `systemctl restart`. **This is not an escalation path** — the source is `home.nix` and the pinned flake inputs, and anyone who can change those can change `system/deploy` itself. But the justification given for filtering PATH is that `sops.environment` is written for a *different consumer* (`sops-install-secrets`, sandboxed, PATH="") and therefore may contain entries that are wrong here. That argument applies to the whole attrset, not just PATH. An allowlist (`GOOGLE_*`, `SOPS_*`, `AWS_*`, `VAULT_*`) is the same amount of jq and does not need revisiting when sops-nix adds a key.
  
  ---
  
  ### 6. nit — the netrc value is validated for emptiness and newlines but not for whitespace
  
  `system/secrets.sh:71`
  
  The multi-line guard is correct and the `wc -l` arithmetic is right (`$( )` has already stripped the trailing newline, `printf '%s'` adds none, so a single-line value counts 0). But a prefixed netrc entry can also be corrupted *within* one line: a token containing spaces, e.g. `tok machine evil.example password tok`, produces a syntactically valid netrc with a second `machine` entry, which would make nix/curl hand credentials to a host of the attacker's choosing.
  
  **Attacker model:** requires write access to `secrets.yaml` **and** KMS encrypt permission — i.e. someone who can already rotate the token to a value of their choosing. Genuinely low value; noted only because the guard next to it is one `case "$val" in *[[:space:]]*) refuse;; esac` away from covering it, and the function is otherwise careful about exactly this class of thing.
  
  (Sub-nit in the same line: `[[ $val == *$'\n'* ]]` would do the multi-line check inside bash instead of piping the plaintext to a PATH-resolved `wc`. Marginal, since `sops`/`install`/`jq` are PATH-resolved too.)
  
  ---
  
  ### 7. nit — `SECRETS` defaults to a CWD-relative path, contradicting the file's own stated contract
  
  `system/secrets.sh:54` — `secrets=${SECRETS-../secrets.yaml}`
  
  The header of the same file states: *"every path is an argument -- no function reaches for a location of its own."* `../secrets.yaml` is a location of its own, and a CWD-relative one. It happens to be right because `deploy` does `cd "$(dirname "$0")"` first, but it means sourcing `secrets.sh` from anywhere else silently reads whatever `../secrets.yaml` resolves to from there. `pacman.sh`, which this file cites as its model, genuinely takes `<dir>` as an argument on every function. Making it `install_secret <secrets-file> <key> <dest> [prefix]`, or just passing the repo root the way `sops_env_for` already does, would make the claim true.
  
  ---
  
  ### Explicitly checked, no finding
  
  - **`sudo install` and the `SUDO`/`SOPS`/`NIX`/`JQ`/`SECRETS` seams (your point 3).** Not an escalation path. Every one of them requires already being the user who runs `deploy`, and that user can equally prepend a directory to `PATH`, edit the repo, or just run `sudo` directly. It is equivalent to the ambient `PATH` exposure any script has, and it follows the convention `pacman.sh` already established. Also worth recording: `sudo` reads its password from `/dev/tty`, not stdin, so having the plaintext on `sudo`'s stdin does not risk it being consumed as a password — and that was true of the old code too.
  - **Failure modes (your point 6).** I walked each: decrypt nonzero → `return 1`; empty → `return 1`; multi-line-with-prefix → `return 1`; `install` fails → `pipefail` propagates; `printf` SIGPIPE → `pipefail` propagates. In every case `install` never runs, so DEST is untouched. Under `set -e` at the top level a nonzero `install_secret` aborts deploy, and the `if !` wrapper correctly scopes errexit suppression to the decrypt itself. Genuine fix, well tested.
  - **`$host` hoisted above the `SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES` guard** (`system/deploy:38`) is correct and the test at `tests/system-secrets.sh:252-259` pins the right invariant (position relative to the guard, not relative to first use).
  - **Missing-key fail-closed paths.** `nix eval` failing → empty array → caught by the `-gt 0` test (and the reasoning about bare `export` succeeding is correct). `sops.environment` present but lacking `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` → `set -u` aborts at line 288 with an ugly message, but aborts. Both fail closed.
  - **Flake evaluation.** `$host` from `uname -n` is interpolated into the flake attrpath but is fully quoted in bash, so no shell injection; a hostile hostname needs root to set. `nix eval` on `..#` copies git-tracked files to the store, which includes the *already-encrypted* `secrets.yaml` — no new disclosure.
  - **`printf '%s%s\n'` normalising trailing newlines.** `$( )` strips all trailing newlines and exactly one is re-added. For the PEM key this is correct (and slightly more robust than the old byte-for-byte pipe). Only latent issue: bash variables cannot carry NUL, so a binary secret would be silently corrupted — neither current secret is binary.

Confirmed: **4 occurrences of the plaintext** in an xtrace run. Both Important findings are real, and the `ALLOW_EXECUTABLES` one is my own fix for last round's nit — I widened a code-execution guard to close an ergonomics gap.

Tests first. Moving the override decision into `secrets.sh` so it's testable at all:

input.old_string: # ── install_secret: decrypt first, install only on success ───────────────────
input.new_string:
# ── sops_env_select: the override branch must not widen anything ─────────────
#
# GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES is not a compatibility toggle. An
# external_account credential config carries credential_source.executable.command,
# an arbitrary command line, and that flag is the interlock Google ships so the
# auth library will not run it. Default-off means a credential config is data;
# on means it is code.
#
# home.nix may set it because the path it names is a writeText store path --
# immutable, and its own comment says so. An operator-supplied path carries no
# such guarantee, so the override branch must not turn the interlock on for it.
mknix '{"GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS":"/nix/store/xxx-wif-hosts.json","GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES":"1","PATH":""}'
got=$(GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/tmp/attacker.json sops_env_select . shiori | sort | tr '\n' ' ')
if [ "$got" = "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/tmp/attacker.json " ]; then
  report "an override does NOT enable ALLOW_EXECUTABLES" ok
else
  report "an override does NOT enable ALLOW_EXECUTABLES" no "got: [$got]"
fi

# Explicitly asking for it is still honoured -- that is the operator deciding,
# which is the whole difference.
got=$(GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/tmp/mine.json GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES=1 \
      sops_env_select . shiori | sort | tr '\n' ' ')
if [ "$got" = "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/tmp/mine.json GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES=1 " ]; then
  report "an explicitly set ALLOW_EXECUTABLES is passed through" ok
else
  report "an explicitly set ALLOW_EXECUTABLES is passed through" no "got: [$got]"
fi

# The decrypt-then-install order is what puts the plaintext in a shell variable,
# and `set -x` traces assignments and builtin arguments. `bash -x system/deploy`
# is how this script gets debugged and its output gets pasted into commit
# messages and issues in a public repo, so an xtrace run must not print the
# token or the mari SSH private key. The old pipeline never held the plaintext
# in the shell and so never had this exposure; keeping the new shape means
# closing it deliberately.
mksops 0 'CANARYVALUE'
rm -f "$D/dest"
trace=$( set -x; install_secret "$D/secrets.yaml" atticPullToken "$D/dest" 'machine attic.ko.ag password '; set +x ) 2>&1
traced=$( { set -x; install_secret "$D/secrets.yaml" atticPullToken "$D/dest" 'machine attic.ko.ag password '; set +x; } 2>&1 )
if ! printf '%s' "$traced" | grep -q CANARYVALUE; then
  report "the plaintext does not reach the xtrace stream" ok
else
  report "the plaintext does not reach the xtrace stream" no \
    "$(printf '%s' "$traced" | grep -c CANARYVALUE) traced line(s) contain the secret"
fi

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# Cases for system/secrets.sh, the sops half of ./deploy.
3	#
4	# Two bugs prompted these, and shiori found both at once.
5	#
6	# 1. ./deploy hardcoded $HOME/.config/sops/gcp-key.json as the GCP credential.
7	#    shiori is the sole WIF host, and the whole point of that migration is that
8	#    it has no decryption key on disk (home.nix's wifHosts comment says so).
9	#    So sops could never decrypt there. home.nix already decides this per host,
10	#    in `sops.environment`, so the fix is to read that rather than re-derive a
11	#    copy of the host list in bash -- which is what these cases pin.
12	#
13	#    The subtlety: that attrset also carries PATH="", which sops-nix sets for
14	#    sops-install-secrets' own sandboxed activation. Exporting it verbatim would
15	#    blank ./deploy's PATH, so it has to be dropped, and a case says so.
16	#
17	# 2. The install pattern was `sops ... | sed ... | sudo install /dev/stdin DEST`.
18	#    All three stages run concurrently, so install created and truncated DEST
19	#    before sops had finished failing, then exited 0 having written nothing. A
20	#    failed deploy therefore destroyed a working netrc and left a 0-byte file
21	#    that looks provisioned -- and `set -e` aborted the script there, so every
22	#    later step silently never ran. That is exactly how shiori ended up with a
23	#    0-byte /etc/determinate/netrc.custom and no /etc/nix/netrc at all.
24	#
25	# Seams, following ../system/pacman.sh: SUDO is `${SUDO-sudo}` (empty means
26	# "write as me"), and SOPS / NIX / JQ stand in for the real binaries.
27	#
28	#   ./tests/system-secrets.sh
29	set -u
30	
31	cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." || exit 1
32	# shellcheck source=../system/secrets.sh
33	. ./system/secrets.sh || { echo "could not source system/secrets.sh" >&2; exit 1; }
34	
35	D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
36	fails=0; n=0
37	
38	# The privilege seam. Not SUDO="" -- these cases run as a normal user, who
39	# cannot chown to root, so a bare `install -o root -g root` fails for a reason
40	# that has nothing to do with what is being tested. This stub drops the
41	# ownership flags and runs the rest as-is; that the file lands root:root 0600 is
42	# ./deploy's business, and root's, not these cases'.
43	cat > "$D/sudo" <<'STUB'
44	#!/usr/bin/env bash
45	out=()
46	while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
47	  case "$1" in
48	    -o|-g) shift 2 ;;
49	    *) out+=("$1"); shift ;;
50	  esac
51	done
52	exec "${out[@]}"
53	STUB
54	chmod +x "$D/sudo"
55	export SUDO="$D/sudo"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# sops helpers for ./deploy. Sourced, never executed: sourcing is what lets
# ../tests/system-secrets.sh drive these against a temp tree instead of /etc.
# Nothing here has an effect at source time, and every path is an argument --
# no function reaches for a location of its own.
#
# The seams are `${VAR-default}`, not `${VAR:-default}`, for the same reason
# ./pacman.sh gives: the tests set SUDO to the empty string to mean "write as
# me", which the :- form would quietly turn back into sudo.

# The sops credential environment for <host>, as KEY=VALUE lines.
#
# home.nix already makes this decision, once, per host: a host in wifHosts gets
# a WIF credential config (a store path, plus the ALLOW_EXECUTABLES flag Google's
# auth library requires for executable-sourced credentials), and every other host
# gets the GCP service-account key under $HOME. Reading `sops.environment` back
# out of the flake is what keeps that decision in one place.
#
# ./deploy used to hardcode the service-account path instead. That made it
# impossible to decrypt on the one WIF host -- the host which, by design, has no
# decryption key on disk at all -- and because the failure landed inside a
# pipeline (see install_secret) it presented as an empty credential file rather
# than as an error.
#
# PATH is dropped. sops-nix puts PATH="" in that attrset for sops-install-secrets'
# own sandboxed activation; exporting it here would blank ./deploy's PATH and
# break every command after the export.
sops_env_for() { # sops_env_for <repo> <host>
  local repo=$1 host=$2
  ${NIX-nix} eval --json "$repo#homeConfigurations.$host.config.sops.environment" \
    | ${JQ-jq} -r 'to_entries[] | select(.key != "PATH") | "\(.key)=\(.value)"'
}

# Decrypt <key> from the secrets file and install it at <dest>, root-owned 0600,
# with <line-prefix> prepended if given.
#
# Decrypt first, install second, and that order is the entire point. The shape
# this replaces was
#
#   sops -d --extract '["k"]' ../secrets.yaml | sed 's#^#prefix #' \
#     | sudo install -m600 -o root -g root /dev/stdin DEST
#
# whose three stages run concurrently: install created and truncated DEST before
# sops had finished failing, then exited 0 having written nothing. So a failed
# deploy did not leave the previous credential in place, it replaced it with a
# 0-byte file that looks provisioned -- and `set -euo pipefail` then stopped the
# script on that line, so every step after it silently never ran.
#
# The plaintext lives in a shell variable and reaches `install` on stdin. It is
# never an argument: /proc/<pid>/cmdline is world-readable, so a secret in argv
# is a secret published to every user on the box for the duration of the call.
# printf is a bash builtin, so nothing is forked to do the write either.
install_secret() { # install_secret <key> <dest> [line-prefix]
  local key=$1 dest=$2 prefix=${3-} secrets=${SECRETS-../secrets.yaml} val

  if ! val=$(${SOPS-sops} -d --extract "[\"$key\"]" "$secrets"); then
    echo "deploy: could not decrypt $key from $secrets" >&2
    return 1
  fi

  # An empty decrypt is the 0-byte-netrc shape arriving by another route. It has
  # to be an error here too, or the file still ends up looking provisioned.
  if [ -z "$val" ]; then
    echo "deploy: $key decrypted to nothing — refusing to install an empty $dest" >&2
    return 1
  fi

  # A prefix is a netrc-entry prefix, and a netrc entry is one line. Prefixing
  # only the first line of a multi-line value would leave a bare token on the
  # second -- a file curl parses happily and wrongly.
  if [ -n "$prefix" ] && [ "$(printf '%s' "$val" | wc -l)" -gt 0 ]; then
    echo "deploy: $key is multi-line; refusing to write it as a prefixed entry in $dest" >&2
    return 1
  fi

  printf '%s%s\n' "$prefix" "$val" \
    | ${SUDO-sudo} install -m600 -o root -g root /dev/stdin "$dest"
}

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# sops helpers for ./deploy. Sourced, never executed: sourcing is what lets
3	# ../tests/system-secrets.sh drive these against a temp tree instead of /etc.
4	# Nothing here has an effect at source time, and every path is an argument --
5	# no function reaches for a location of its own.
6	#
7	# The seams are `${VAR-default}`, not `${VAR:-default}`, for the same reason
8	# ./pacman.sh gives: the tests set SUDO to the empty string to mean "write as
9	# me", which the :- form would quietly turn back into sudo.
10	
11	# The sops credential environment for <host>, as KEY=VALUE lines.
12	#
13	# home.nix already makes this decision, once, per host: a host in wifHosts gets
14	# a WIF credential config (a store path, plus the ALLOW_EXECUTABLES flag Google's
15	# auth library requires for executable-sourced credentials), and every other host
16	# gets the GCP service-account key under $HOME. Reading `sops.environment` back
17	# out of the flake is what keeps that decision in one place.
18	#
19	# ./deploy used to hardcode the service-account path instead. That made it
20	# impossible to decrypt on the one WIF host -- the host which, by design, has no
21	# decryption key on disk at all -- and because the failure landed inside a
22	# pipeline (see install_secret) it presented as an empty credential file rather
23	# than as an error.
24	#
25	# PATH is dropped. sops-nix puts PATH="" in that attrset for sops-install-secrets'
26	# own sandboxed activation; exporting it here would blank ./deploy's PATH and
27	# break every command after the export.
28	sops_env_for() { # sops_env_for <repo> <host>
29	  local repo=$1 host=$2
30	  ${NIX-nix} eval --json "$repo#homeConfigurations.$host.config.sops.environment" \
31	    | ${JQ-jq} -r 'to_entries[] | select(.key != "PATH") | "\(.key)=\(.value)"'
32	}
33	
34	# The same, unless the caller set GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, in which case
35	# that wins -- for deliberately deploying with some other credential.
36	#
37	# What this deliberately does NOT do is default
38	# GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES on for that override. That flag is
39	# not a compatibility toggle: an external_account credential config carries
40	# `credential_source.executable.command`, an arbitrary command line, and the flag
41	# is the interlock Google ships so the auth library will not run it. Off means a
42	# credential config is data; on means it is code.
43	#
44	# home.nix sets it because the path it names is a writeText store path --
45	# immutable and root-owned, and its comment says as much. An operator-supplied
46	# path carries no such guarantee, and credential configs are documented as
47	# safe-to-commit artifacts, so they circulate: pasted into an issue, downloaded
48	# during a bootstrap, sitting in a world-writable directory. Turning the
49	# interlock on for a path someone was handed would make running deploy with it
50	# code execution as the user -- and in the bootstrap path, one NOPASSWD sudo
51	# away from root.
52	#
53	# So an override may still ask for it, explicitly, and that is the operator
54	# deciding. It is just not decided for them.
55	sops_env_select() { # sops_env_select <repo> <host>
56	  if [ -n "${GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS-}" ]; then
57	    printf 'GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=%s\n' "$GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS"
58	    [ -z "${GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES-}" ] \
59	      || printf 'GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES=%s\n' \
60	           "$GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES"
61	    return 0
62	  fi
63	  sops_env_for "$1" "$2"
64	}
65	
66	# Decrypt <key> from <secrets-file> and install it at <dest>, root-owned 0600,
67	# with <line-prefix> prepended if given.
68	#
69	# Decrypt first, install second, and that order is the entire point. The shape
70	# this replaces was
71	#
72	#   sops -d --extract '["k"]' ../secrets.yaml | sed 's#^#prefix #' \
73	#     | sudo install -m600 -o root -g root /dev/stdin DEST
74	#
75	# whose three stages run concurrently: install created and truncated DEST before
76	# sops had finished failing, then exited 0 having written nothing. So a failed
77	# deploy did not leave the previous credential in place, it replaced it with a
78	# 0-byte file that looks provisioned -- and `set -euo pipefail` then stopped the
79	# script on that line, so every step after it silently never ran.
80	#
81	# The plaintext lives in a shell variable and reaches `install` on stdin. It is
82	# never an argument: /proc/<pid>/cmdline is world-readable, so a secret in argv
83	# is a secret published to every user on the box for the duration of the call.
84	# printf is a bash builtin, so nothing is forked to do the write either.
85	# Tracing is off for the whole of the inner function and restored after, which
86	# is the price of holding the plaintext in a shell variable at all. `set -x`
87	# traces assignments and the arguments of builtins, so `bash -x system/deploy`
88	# -- how this script gets debugged, and whose output gets pasted into commit
89	# messages and issues in a public repo -- would otherwise print the attic pull
90	# token and the mari SSH private key in full to stderr. The pipeline this
91	# replaced never held the plaintext in the shell, so it never had that exposure;
92	# the new shape has to close it deliberately. One restore point, so no early
93	# return can skip it.
94	install_secret() { # install_secret <secrets-file> <key> <dest> [line-prefix]
95	  local xtrace=""
96	  case $- in *x*) xtrace=1; set +x ;; esac
97	  _install_secret "$@"
98	  local rc=$?
99	  [ -z "$xtrace" ] || set -x
100	  return "$rc"
101	}
102	
103	_install_secret() { # not called directly; see install_secret above
104	  local secrets=$1 key=$2 dest=$3 prefix=${4-} val
105	
106	  if ! val=$(${SOPS-sops} -d --extract "[\"$key\"]" "$secrets"); then
107	    echo "deploy: could not decrypt $key from $secrets" >&2
108	    return 1
109	  fi
110	
111	  # An empty decrypt is the 0-byte-netrc shape arriving by another route. It has
112	  # to be an error here too, or the file still ends up looking provisioned.
113	  if [ -z "$val" ]; then
114	    echo "deploy: $key decrypted to nothing — refusing to install an empty $dest" >&2
115	    return 1
116	  fi
117	
118	  # A prefix is a netrc-entry prefix, and a netrc entry is one line. Prefixing
119	  # only the first line of a multi-line value would leave a bare token on the
120	  # second -- a file curl parses happily and wrongly.
121	  if [ -n "$prefix" ] && [ "$(printf '%s' "$val" | wc -l)" -gt 0 ]; then
122	    echo "deploy: $key is multi-line; refusing to write it as a prefixed entry in $dest" >&2
123	    return 1
124	  fi
125	
126	  printf '%s%s\n' "$prefix" "$val" \
127	    | ${SUDO-sudo} install -m600 -o root -g root /dev/stdin "$dest"
128	}

input.old_string:
# An explicit GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS still wins, for the case where you
# are deliberately deploying with some other credential.
#
# ALLOW_EXECUTABLES is set alongside it rather than left to the caller. home.nix
# pairs those two for WIF, and the most natural way to use this override on a WIF
# host -- pointing it at a wif-hosts.json by hand -- would otherwise have Google's
# auth library refuse the executable-sourced credential. Setting it is harmless
# for a service-account key, which ignores it, so the pair stays together.
if [ -n "${GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS-}" ]; then
  echo "system/deploy: using GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS from the environment"
  export GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS
  export GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES="${GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES-1}"
else
  # mapfile rather than word-splitting: a credential path could contain spaces,
  # and these lines are KEY=VALUE pairs meant for `env`, not for the shell.
  #
  # No `||` on the mapfile, deliberately. mapfile's exit status is mapfile's own
  # and never the process substitution's -- the same trap the pacman_wants call
  # above documents -- so a `|| exit` there would be dead code claiming a check
  # it does not perform. A failed `nix eval` writes to stderr and nothing to
  # stdout, so it arrives here as an empty array, which the length test catches.
  mapfile -t sops_env < <(sops_env_for .. "$host")
  # Load-bearing beyond the error message: `export "${empty_array[@]}"` expands
  # to zero words, and bare `export` prints the whole environment and succeeds.
  [ "${#sops_env[@]}" -gt 0 ] || {
    echo "system/deploy: no sops.environment for $host — nix eval failed, or the host has none." >&2
    echo "system/deploy: nix's own error, if any, is above." >&2
    exit 1
  }
  export "${sops_env[@]}"
fi

restore() { git checkout -- system/secrets.sh; }
trap restore EXIT

sed -i 's/^  case \$- in \*x\*) xtrace=1; set +x ;; esac$/  case $- in *x*) xtrace=1 ;; esac/' system/secrets.sh

./tests/system-secrets.sh 2>&1 | grep -E '^(ok 17|FAIL 17|[0-9]+/)'
restore

sed -i 's/install -m600 -o root -g root/install -m600/' system/secrets.sh

restore

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# sops helpers for ./deploy. Sourced, never executed: sourcing is what lets
# ../tests/system-secrets.sh drive these against a temp tree instead of /etc.
# Nothing here has an effect at source time, and every path is an argument --
# no function reaches for a location of its own.
#
# The seams are `${VAR-default}`, not `${VAR:-default}`, for the same reason
# ./pacman.sh gives: the tests set SUDO to the empty string to mean "write as
# me", which the :- form would quietly turn back into sudo.

# The sops credential environment for <host>, as KEY=VALUE lines.
#
# home.nix already makes this decision, once, per host: a host in wifHosts gets
# a WIF credential config (a store path, plus the ALLOW_EXECUTABLES flag Google's
# auth library requires for executable-sourced credentials), and every other host
# gets the GCP service-account key under $HOME. Reading `sops.environment` back
# out of the flake is what keeps that decision in one place.
#
# ./deploy used to hardcode the service-account path instead. That made it
# impossible to decrypt on the one WIF host -- the host which, by design, has no
# decryption key on disk at all -- and because the failure landed inside a
# pipeline (see install_secret) it presented as an empty credential file rather
# than as an error.
#
# PATH is dropped. sops-nix puts PATH="" in that attrset for sops-install-secrets'
# own sandboxed activation; exporting it here would blank ./deploy's PATH and
# break every command after the export.
sops_env_for() { # sops_env_for <repo> <host>
  local repo=$1 host=$2
  ${NIX-nix} eval --json "$repo#homeConfigurations.$host.config.sops.environment" \
    | ${JQ-jq} -r 'to_entries[] | select(.key != "PATH") | "\(.key)=\(.value)"'
}

# Decrypt <key> from the secrets file and install it at <dest>, root-owned 0600,
# with <line-prefix> prepended if given.
#
# Decrypt first, install second, and that order is the entire point. The shape
# this replaces was
#
#   sops -d --extract '["k"]' ../secrets.yaml | sed 's#^#prefix #' \
#     | sudo install -m600 -o root -g root /dev/stdin DEST
#
# whose three stages run concurrently: install created and truncated DEST before
# sops had finished failing, then exited 0 having written nothing. So a failed
# deploy did not leave the previous credential in place, it replaced it with a
# 0-byte file that looks provisioned -- and `set -euo pipefail` then stopped the
# script on that line, so every step after it silently never ran.
#
# The plaintext lives in a shell variable and reaches `install` on stdin. It is
# never an argument: /proc/<pid>/cmdline is world-readable, so a secret in argv
# is a secret published to every user on the box for the duration of the call.
# printf is a bash builtin, so nothing is forked to do the write either.
install_secret() { # install_secret <key> <dest> [line-prefix]
  local key=$1 dest=$2 prefix=${3-} secrets=${SECRETS-../secrets.yaml} val

  if ! val=$(${SOPS-sops} -d --extract "[\"$key\"]" "$secrets"); then
    echo "deploy: could not decrypt $key from $secrets" >&2
    return 1
  fi

  # An empty decrypt is the 0-byte-netrc shape arriving by another route. It has
  # to be an error here too, or the file still ends up looking provisioned.
  if [ -z "$val" ]; then
    echo "deploy: $key decrypted to nothing — refusing to install an empty $dest" >&2
    return 1
  fi

  # A prefix is a netrc-entry prefix, and a netrc entry is one line. Prefixing
  # only the first line of a multi-line value would leave a bare token on the
  # second -- a file curl parses happily and wrongly.
  if [ -n "$prefix" ] && [ "$(printf '%s' "$val" | wc -l)" -gt 0 ]; then
    echo "deploy: $key is multi-line; refusing to write it as a prefixed entry in $dest" >&2
    return 1
  fi

  printf '%s%s\n' "$prefix" "$val" \
    | ${SUDO-sudo} install -m600 -o root -g root /dev/stdin "$dest"
}

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# sops helpers for ./deploy. Sourced, never executed: sourcing is what lets
# ../tests/system-secrets.sh drive these against a temp tree instead of /etc.
# Nothing here has an effect at source time, and every path is an argument --
# no function reaches for a location of its own.
#
# The seams are `${VAR-default}`, not `${VAR:-default}`, for the same reason
# ./pacman.sh gives: the tests set SUDO to the empty string to mean "write as
# me", which the :- form would quietly turn back into sudo.

# The sops credential environment for <host>, as KEY=VALUE lines.
#
# home.nix already makes this decision, once, per host: a host in wifHosts gets
# a WIF credential config (a store path, plus the ALLOW_EXECUTABLES flag Google's
# auth library requires for executable-sourced credentials), and every other host
# gets the GCP service-account key under $HOME. Reading `sops.environment` back
# out of the flake is what keeps that decision in one place.
#
# ./deploy used to hardcode the service-account path instead. That made it
# impossible to decrypt on the one WIF host -- the host which, by design, has no
# decryption key on disk at all -- and because the failure landed inside a
# pipeline (see install_secret) it presented as an empty credential file rather
# than as an error.
#
# PATH is dropped. sops-nix puts PATH="" in that attrset for sops-install-secrets'
# own sandboxed activation; exporting it here would blank ./deploy's PATH and
# break every command after the export.
sops_env_for() { # sops_env_for <repo> <host>
  local repo=$1 host=$2
  ${NIX-nix} eval --json "$repo#homeConfigurations.$host.config.sops.environment" \
    | ${JQ-jq} -r 'to_entries[] | select(.key != "PATH") | "\(.key)=\(.value)"'
}

# The same, unless the caller set GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, in which case
# that wins -- for deliberately deploying with some other credential.
#
# What this deliberately does NOT do is default
# GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES on for that override. That flag is
# not a compatibility toggle: an external_account credential config carries
# `credential_source.executable.command`, an arbitrary command line, and the flag
# is the interlock Google ships so the auth library will not run it. Off means a
# credential config is data; on means it is code.
#
# home.nix sets it because the path it names is a writeText store path --
# immutable, and its own comment says as much. An operator-supplied path carries
# no such guarantee, and credential configs are documented as safe-to-commit
# artifacts, so they circulate: pasted into an issue, downloaded during a
# bootstrap, sitting in a world-writable directory. Turning the interlock on for
# a path someone was handed would make running deploy with it code execution as
# the user -- and in the bootstrap path, one NOPASSWD sudo away from root.
#
# So an override may still ask for it, explicitly. That is the operator
# deciding; it is just not decided for them.
sops_env_select() { # sops_env_select <repo> <host>
  if [ -n "${GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS-}" ]; then
    printf 'GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=%s\n' "$GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS"
    [ -z "${GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES-}" ] \
      || printf 'GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES=%s\n' \
           "$GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES"
    return 0
  fi
  sops_env_for "$1" "$2"
}

# Decrypt <key> from the secrets file and install it at <dest>, root-owned 0600,
# with <line-prefix> prepended if given.
#
# Decrypt first, install second, and that order is the entire point. The shape
# this replaces was
#
#   sops -d --extract '["k"]' ../secrets.yaml | sed 's#^#prefix #' \
#     | sudo install -m600 -o root -g root /dev/stdin DEST
#
# whose three stages run concurrently: install created and truncated DEST before
# sops had finished failing, then exited 0 having written nothing. So a failed
# deploy did not leave the previous credential in place, it replaced it with a
# 0-byte file that looks provisioned -- and `set -euo pipefail` then stopped the
# script on that line, so every step after it silently never ran.
#
# The plaintext lives in a shell variable and reaches `install` on stdin. It is
# never an argument: /proc/<pid>/cmdline is world-readable, so a secret in argv
# is a secret published to every user on the box for the duration of the call.
# printf is a bash builtin, so nothing is forked to do the write either.
install_secret() { # install_secret <key> <dest> [line-prefix]
  local key=$1 dest=$2 prefix=${3-} secrets=${SECRETS-../secrets.yaml} val

  if ! val=$(${SOPS-sops} -d --extract "[\"$key\"]" "$secrets"); then
    echo "deploy: could not decrypt $key from $secrets" >&2
    return 1
  fi

  # An empty decrypt is the 0-byte-netrc shape arriving by another route. It has
  # to be an error here too, or the file still ends up looking provisioned.
  if [ -z "$val" ]; then
    echo "deploy: $key decrypted to nothing — refusing to install an empty $dest" >&2
    return 1
  fi

  # A prefix is a netrc-entry prefix, and a netrc entry is one line. Prefixing
  # only the first line of a multi-line value would leave a bare token on the
  # second -- a file curl parses happily and wrongly.
  if [ -n "$prefix" ] && [ "$(printf '%s' "$val" | wc -l)" -gt 0 ]; then
    echo "deploy: $key is multi-line; refusing to write it as a prefixed entry in $dest" >&2
    return 1
  fi

  printf '%s%s\n' "$prefix" "$val" \
    | ${SUDO-sudo} install -m600 -o root -g root /dev/stdin "$dest"
}

content.text:
Full suite running. Where this landed:

**Both Important findings were mine, and one was self-inflicted.**

1. **`ALLOW_EXECUTABLES` defaulted on in the override branch** — I added that last round to close a nit, and in doing so widened a code-execution interlock. An `external_account` credential config contains `credential_source.executable.command`; that flag is what stops the auth library running it. `home.nix` may set it because the path it names is an immutable store path — an operator-supplied path carries no such guarantee, and credential configs are documented as safe-to-commit, so they circulate. Now the override passes through an *explicitly* set flag but never defaults it on. Moved into `sops_env_select` in `secrets.sh` so it's testable at all.

2. **`set -x` leaked the plaintext** — holding the secret in a shell variable is what makes decrypt-before-install possible, and it's also what makes `bash -x system/deploy` print the attic token and the mari SSH private key to stderr. Measured it: 4 occurrences. The old pipeline never had this. Tracing is now suppressed for the secret's lifetime with a single restore point.

Also closed the reviewer's test gaps: the `sudo` stub now *records* `-o`/`-g` instead of silently dropping them (deleting them passed every case before), and there's a case for the overwrite path, not just create.

All three new assertions mutation-tested — each fails when I reintroduce the corresponding bug.

**Process failure worth flagging:** my first mutation script restored with `git checkout -- system/secrets.sh`, which discarded my *uncommitted* changes rather than the mutation. I lost and had to rewrite the work. The second script backs up the working-tree copy instead.

**Not fixed, recorded:** non-atomic write (a failed *write* still leaves a truncated file — narrow, reviewer wouldn't block); allowlist-vs-denylist for `sops.environment` filtering (an allowlist would silently drop a future key we need, turning a loud failure quiet); whitespace-in-token netrc injection (needs KMS encrypt access, i.e. someone who can already choose the token).

library running it. home.nix may set it because the path it names is an immutable
writeText store path; an operator-supplied path carries no such guarantee, and
credential configs are documented as safe-to-commit artifacts, so they circulate.

install_secret passed every case while the files landed owned by whoever ran
deploy. It records them now, and a case asserts root. Each of the three new
security assertions was mutation-tested: reintroduce the bug, watch that case and
only that case fail.

CWD-relative path, which makes this file's own "every path is an argument" claim
true.

*write*, as opposed to a failed decrypt, can still truncate); the PATH filter is a

encrypt access -- i.e. someone who can already choose the token.

2	
3	shiori has been building everything locally since the WIF migration. Every nix
4	invocation on it warns
5	
6	  unable to download 'https://attic.ko.ag/kube/nix-cache-info': HTTP error 401
7	
8	and then builds, because nix fails open on a substituter it cannot authenticate
9	to. That silently defeats the entire reason `hms` waits for CI: the switch is
10	supposed to be a download of the closure the runner already pushed to attic.
11	
12	Two bugs, and the second is what kept the first quiet.
13	
14	**The credential.** ./deploy hardcoded $HOME/.config/sops/gcp-key.json. shiori is
15	the sole WIF host, and the point of that migration is that it has no decryption
16	key on disk at all -- home.nix's wifHosts comment says so in as many words. So
17	sops could never decrypt there. home.nix already makes this choice per host, in
18	`sops.environment`, so ./secrets.sh now reads that back out of the flake instead
19	of keeping a second copy of the host list in bash. An explicit
20	GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS still wins, and carries ALLOW_EXECUTABLES with it
21	rather than splitting a pair home.nix deliberately keeps together.
22	
23	One trap in doing that: the same attrset carries PATH="", which sops-nix sets for
24	sops-install-secrets' own sandboxed activation. Exporting it verbatim would blank
25	./deploy's PATH and break every command after the export, so it is dropped, and a
26	case pins that.

29	its three stages concurrently, so install created and truncated DEST before sops
30	had finished failing, then exited 0 having written nothing. A failed deploy did
31	not leave the previous credential alone -- it replaced it with a 0-byte file that
32	looks provisioned. `set -euo pipefail` then stopped the script on that line, so
33	everything after it never ran. That is precisely the state shiori was in: a

39	plaintext still never reaches argv: it goes to install on stdin via bash's
40	builtin printf, since /proc/<pid>/cmdline is world-readable.

43	one line, and prefixing only the first would leave a bare token on the second,
44	which curl parses happily and wrongly.

system/deploy: take the sops credential from the flake, and decrypt before installing

shiori has been building everything locally since the WIF migration. Every nix
invocation on it warns

  unable to download 'https://attic.ko.ag/kube/nix-cache-info': HTTP error 401

and then builds, because nix fails open on a substituter it cannot authenticate
to. That silently defeats the entire reason `hms` waits for CI: the switch is
supposed to be a download of the closure the runner already pushed to attic.

Two bugs, and the second is what kept the first quiet.

**The credential.** ./deploy hardcoded $HOME/.config/sops/gcp-key.json. shiori is
the sole WIF host, and the point of that migration is that it has no decryption
key on disk at all -- home.nix's wifHosts comment says so in as many words. So
sops could never decrypt there. home.nix already makes this choice per host, in
`sops.environment`, so ./secrets.sh now reads that back out of the flake instead
of keeping a second copy of the host list in bash. An explicit
GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS still wins, and carries ALLOW_EXECUTABLES with it
rather than splitting a pair home.nix deliberately keeps together.

One trap in doing that: the same attrset carries PATH="", which sops-nix sets for
sops-install-secrets' own sandboxed activation. Exporting it verbatim would blank
./deploy's PATH and break every command after the export, so it is dropped, and a
case pins that.

**The install pattern.** `sops ... | sed ... | sudo install /dev/stdin DEST` runs
its three stages concurrently, so install created and truncated DEST before sops
had finished failing, then exited 0 having written nothing. A failed deploy did
not leave the previous credential alone -- it replaced it with a 0-byte file that
looks provisioned. `set -euo pipefail` then stopped the script on that line, so
everything after it never ran. That is precisely the state shiori was in: a
0-byte /etc/determinate/netrc.custom, no /etc/nix/netrc at all (deploy writes it
two lines later), no mari builder key, and an unrestarted nix-daemon.

install_secret decrypts into a variable first and installs only on success, and
treats an empty decrypt as a failure rather than as something worth writing. The
plaintext still never reaches argv: it goes to install on stdin via bash's
builtin printf, since /proc/<pid>/cmdline is world-readable.

Also refuses a multi-line value where a line prefix was given -- a netrc entry is
one line, and prefixing only the first would leave a bare token on the second,
which curl parses happily and wrongly.

**$host moves to the top**, which review caught and this commit would otherwise
have broken: it was assigned inside the else arm of the SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES guard,
and the new sops block reads it unconditionally. Under `set -u` that made
`SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES=1 ./system/deploy` -- the documented way to re-run the
non-package half -- abort on an unbound variable after the etc/ copy and before
every credential it installs.

No `||` on the mapfile, also deliberately: mapfile's exit status is its own and
never the process substitution's, the same trap the pacman_wants call above
already documents. A failed `nix eval` arrives as an empty array instead, which
the length test catches -- and that test is load-bearing beyond its message,
because `export "${empty[@]}"` expands to zero words and bare `export` prints the
environment and succeeds.

tests/system-secrets.sh drives all of it through the ./pacman.sh seam convention
(SUDO is ${SUDO-sudo}, plus SOPS / NIX / JQ). Two of its cases were verified by
mutation rather than assumption: removing -m600 fails the mode case, and removing
the decrypt exit-status check fails the untouched-file case. Verified separately
against the real flake on shiori: sops_env_for returns the two WIF vars with no
PATH, and a real decrypt through that env exits 0.

Docs were actively misleading and are corrected: nix-binary-cache.md omitted
shiori from the wired-hosts list and still told you the deploy needs your
gcp-key.json.

Still outstanding: mise.toml's `sops` task hardcodes the same service-account
path, so it remains broken on shiori for this same reason.

This does not fix the running host -- ./system/deploy has to be run for that.

Two things security review caught, both introduced here:

The override branch must NOT default GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES on
-- that was an earlier revision of this commit closing an ergonomics nit by
widening a code-execution interlock. An external_account credential config carries
credential_source.executable.command, and that flag is what stops Google's auth
library running it. home.nix may set it because the path it names is an immutable
writeText store path; an operator-supplied path carries no such guarantee, and
credential configs are documented as safe-to-commit artifacts, so they circulate.
An override may still ask for it explicitly. sops_env_select owns that choice, in
./secrets.sh, so it is testable.

And holding the plaintext in a shell variable -- which is what makes
decrypt-before-install possible -- is traced by `set -x`. `bash -x system/deploy`
printed the attic token and the mari SSH private key in full to stderr; measured,
four occurrences. The pipeline this replaces never had that exposure. Tracing is
now suppressed for the secret's lifetime, with one restore point so no early
return can skip it.

The test's sudo stub also used to discard -o/-g silently, so deleting them from
install_secret passed every case while the files landed owned by whoever ran
deploy. It records them now, and a case asserts root. Each of the three new
security assertions was mutation-tested: reintroduce the bug, watch that case and
only that case fail.

install_secret takes the secrets file as an argument rather than defaulting to a
CWD-relative path, which makes this file's own "every path is an argument" claim
true.

Deliberately not fixed, for the record: the write is still non-atomic (a failed
*write*, as opposed to a failed decrypt, can still truncate); the PATH filter is a
denylist rather than an allowlist, because an allowlist would silently drop a
future sops-nix key we need and turn a loud failure into a quiet one; and a token
containing whitespace could inject a second netrc entry, which requires KMS
encrypt access -- i.e. someone who can already choose the token.

What I changed:

I measured 4 plaintext occurrences under `set -x` before and 0 after via a test case. Check: is the suppression actually complete — does anything leak before `set +x` takes effect (the wrapper's own invocation line, the argument expansion), does `BASH_XTRACEFD` or `SHELLOPTS` defeat it, does an `ERR` trap or `set -e` exit skip the restore, and is restoring unconditionally correct when the caller had xtrace off?

I did NOT fix three of your nits, deliberately: the non-atomic write, the denylist-vs-allowlist on `sops.environment` filtering, and the whitespace-in-token netrc injection. Reasons are in the commit message. Say so if you think any of those three was the wrong call given what else changed.

`git show a586a81` — or diff aec8243..a586a81 to see only what changed in response to you.

What I changed:

1. **ALLOW_EXECUTABLES.** The override branch moved out of `system/deploy` into a new `sops_env_select` in `system/secrets.sh`, specifically so it could be tested. It now emits `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` from the environment, and emits `GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES` only if the caller set it explicitly — never defaulted to 1. Check: does that actually close the path you described, or did moving it introduce a new way for the flag to arrive? In particular, `deploy` still does `export "${sops_env[@]}"` over whatever that function emits, and I want to know whether an ambient `GOOGLE_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNT_ALLOW_EXECUTABLES=1` with no `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` can now reach the flake branch and pair itself with the store-path credential (harmless?) or anything worse.

2. **xtrace.** `install_secret` is now a thin wrapper that records `case $- in *x*)`, does `set +x`, calls `_install_secret "$@"`, restores, and returns the inner status. I measured 4 plaintext occurrences under `set -x` before and 0 after via a test case. Check: is the suppression actually complete — does anything leak before `set +x` takes effect (the wrapper's own invocation line, the argument expansion), does `BASH_XTRACEFD` or `SHELLOPTS` defeat it, does an `ERR` trap or `set -e` exit skip the restore, and is restoring unconditionally correct when the caller had xtrace off?

Also changed, and worth a skeptical look since they touch the same code: `install_secret` now takes the secrets file as its first argument (signature is `<secrets-file> <key> <dest> [prefix]`), and the test's `sudo` stub now records `-o`/`-g` into a file instead of discarding them, with a case asserting `-o root -g root`.

I did NOT fix three of your nits, deliberately: the non-atomic write, the denylist-vs-allowlist on `sops.environment` filtering, and the whitespace-in-token netrc injection. Reasons are in the commit message. Say so if you think any of those three was the wrong call given what else changed.

Report as before: Critical / Important / nit, concrete failure scenarios, and say plainly if the two findings are now closed.

entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

Security reviewer resumed to verify its own findings — it has the full context, which a fresh reviewer wouldn't.

State on `a586a81`:

| Angle | Coverage |
|---|---|
| correctness | panel, clean, 0 findings |
| error-handling | panel, clean, 0 findings |
| type-design | panel, clean, 0 findings |
| security | panel died 3rd time → original reviewer verifying |

Verification: 14/14 suites green, `system-secrets` 18/18, `nix build` clean, real-flake smoke test still exits 0, and all three new security assertions mutation-tested.

Worth noting for your stored drovr memory: the panel has now lost an angle in **three consecutive rounds** — correctness once, security twice. Your note says "the correctness reviewer dies"; the real pattern is that *some* angle drops most rounds, so the note should be widened. The review discipline treats two consecutive lost dimensions as a terminating condition precisely because more rounds stop measuring anything, which is why I'm covering gaps with substitutes rather than re-running.

One thing I'd flag about my own process: I lost work this session by restoring a mutation with `git checkout --` on a file with uncommitted changes. No harm done — I rewrote it and the tests caught the intermediate breakage — but it also produced a stray `atticPullToken` file in the worktree, which I accounted for byte-for-byte (stub value, no real secret) and deleted.
